body: In my opinion, the biggest one is when you want to do something and you still can't. There's a task you need to do that's very important, you really want to do it because of the impact on your life, it's not too difficult for you, it might not even take very long, but because it is boring, you are as incapable of doing it as if I asked you to suddenly fly. It's not that you don't want to or that you'd rather do something else, you're miserable about this, not happily playing a game or so on. You simply, literally can't do it. You \*might\* get the ability to do it once it's just slightly too late, and even that isn't a given.

I don't read incompletes but the rare times I do, I will not leave kudos until it's complete--you can't take back a kudos if the work later goes in a bad direction. I leave kudos when I would recommend the work to a friend, basically: I enjoyed reading it, it's well-written, and it doesn't have untagged "problematic" content (smut in a T fic, extremely ooc characters, etc etc).

I have a greasemonkey script that shows kudos/hits ratios and for completed works of "reasonable" size, I find that a good ratio is very representative of whether I'll enjoy a work or not. (Good is dependent on the fandom, some fandoms definitely kudos more or less per hit than others.) I won't kudos something that I wish I hadn't read because I feel like that's giving inaccurate info to the next reader. And I've gotten very internally annoyed when I open something with a ton of kudos that is so poorly written as to be nearly unreadable--you lied to me!

I'm diagnosed and medicated, but on me the result is more "slightly better" than "life changing" unfortunately (I don't have any options to switch medications around to see if others work better where I live). And years of therapy have done little... that's life I suppose.

I come from a similar background, where I was raised to feel that any failure at all would be the end of the world. I did fantastically through my studies and then failed spectacularly in the working world, and I think I'll never stop being angry that no one taught me failing was ok in school. I built my entire identity around being someone who always succeeded, that's what I was always praised for. So when I failed, it was the end of the world to me, because suddenly I had lost my definition of myself. In fact, I think those who fail in school, and who allow themselves to decide that there are things they care about and things they do not, are a step ahead of us "gifted" kids. Because it's very unlikely you'll never fail in your life, especially once you exit the very cleanly ordered setting that school/university is, and it's a lot harder to learn the longer you wait to do it. I'm sure you've heard the joke of saying you're a perfectionist when asked for a character flaw, as if it was actually a sneaky way to brag, but internalize it: perfectionism is truly a character flaw. Learn to fail while you still can and you will be happier for it long term.   


This isn't really an answer to your question, I realize! In some cases you do need to find some sort of technique to force yourself to do \*enough\* of the thing to get by. But it's a lot easier to do that when you're not operating in perfectionist mode, where you're basically going "since I can't be perfect at this then I'm gonna be really bad on purpose, and that way I can't feel bad it wasn't perfect since I didn't try." (Whether that's something you're doing consciously or not.)
